paper_title: Constraining hidden photons via atomic force microscope measurements and the Plimpton-Lawton experiment
notes: Dark photon (hidden photon) kinetically mixed with the photon; canonical variable chi reported directly (paper's own chi, y-axis is log10 chi). Headline result is the AFM (atomic-force-microscope Casimir-force) bound shown as the red curve in Fig. 1 and Fig. 6 (curve labeled a1=62nm, a2=100nm, DeltaM/M=1%), extracted from the vector figure different_separations.pdf in the arXiv e-print. The intro explicitly frames this as the paper's exclusion 'covering mass scales in the 0.1-10 eV range and chi >~ 10^-0.5, as shown by the red curve in Fig. 1' - matching this extraction (mass 0.1-9 eV, chi minimum ~10^-0.47 near m~1.5 eV). The excluded region lies ABOVE this U-shaped boundary curve; endpoints truncated at chi=1 (log10 chi=0). Axes calibrated from matplotlib tick labels (x: log10 m/eV, y: log10 chi); calibration cross-checked against the paper's quoted chi>~10^-0.5 minimum. This is a lab-based force/Coulomb-law test, not a dark-matter search, so no density rescaling applies (dm_density_assumed=null). No formal statistical CL is stated; the bound follows from ~1-sigma experimental-uncertainty compatibility (DeltaM/M=1%) via the linear inversion of Eqs. 19-22; confidence_level set to 0.95 nominally. CAVEAT: the paper derives a SECOND independent new bound from the Plimpton-Lawton concentric-shell experiment (purple curve, Fig. 7/Fig. 8, from Eq. 26; reaches chi~10^-4 near m~10^-6 eV over m~10^-11 to 10^2 eV). Both are 'our bounds'; I chose the AFM curve because the title leads with it, the intro/abstract quote its numbers, and Sections II-III develop it as the paper's central novel analysis. If the compilation instead digitised the Plimpton-Lawton bound, this curve would be wrong.
